# Overview, notation and policies {#sec-model-overview}

This chapter opens the book. It says what the shared model is, how a run is organised, and in which order the
model computes. It fixes the notation, the units and the conventions that every later chapter uses. It then
explains the first two blocks of the model: the **header** of macro series (block M0) and the **policies**
(block M1 and its adjustments A1), which turn the scenario inputs into a price signal for every year, fuel and
sector.

The model is shared by two implementations. **Excel-AI** (the Excel prototype, tab
[CPAT Excel-AI](../CPAT_ai_documentation_html/02_Mitigation_Prototype.html)) computes each equation in workbook
rows. **CPAT Python** (Coded CPAT, tab
[CPAT Python](../CPAT_coded_documentation_html/02_How_it_works.html#sec-blocks)) computes the same equation in one
function. Both use the same variable codes and the same order of calculation, and CPAT Python is checked against
Excel-AI code by code and year by year.

## What the model is {#sec-ov-what}

The model is the mitigation module of the IMF and World Bank **Climate Policy Assessment Tool (CPAT)**, together
with its distribution module. It answers one question: **what do carbon pricing and related policies do to energy
prices, energy use, emissions, government revenue, GDP and households, year by year to 2041?**

It follows the method of legacy CPAT, described in the methodology
([methodology, section 3.1.2](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#sec-ExecSummMethodology)): a
reduced-form model in which fuel use responds to income, prices and efficiency, with a techno-economic model of
the power sector. It departs from legacy CPAT only where legacy has a bug (always fixed) or where a decision was
taken and recorded (the boxes "Differences from legacy CPAT" list them).

| | |
|---|---|
| **Policies in** | Carbon tax; new emissions trading system (ETS) with a cap; feebates; energy efficiency regulations (as shadow prices); fuel excises (fuel price reform); consumer subsidy, price-control and producer subsidy phase-outs; methane fee; existing carbon taxes and ETS; power-sector policies; road vehicle policies |
| **Results out** | Retail energy prices; fuel use in 16 subsectors and 9 fuels; electricity generation, capacity and prices; revenue; CO2, other greenhouse gases and local air pollutants; GDP effects; the gap to the country's NDC; household effects by decile |
| **Country** | One country at a time in Excel-AI, any number of countries at once in CPAT Python. Equations contain no country numbers: every country value comes from the data, looked up by the country code |

The methodology's own summary of the policies CPAT can assess is in its user guide
([methodology, section 1.1](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/01_User_Guide.html#sec-1_1)).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** workbook `CPAT-AI-Mitigation-Prototype_v<version>.xlsm`. The model is sheet Mitigation, run top to
  bottom, one section per step with the section numbers of legacy CPAT (0 header, 1 policies, 2 prices, 3 power,
  5-8 sectors, 11 totals, 12 revenues, 13-15 emissions, 16-18 GDP, indicators, welfare), and sheet Distribution.
  The inputs are on ScenarioDefinition (the rows of legacy MTInputs), Settings, Constants and Manual inputs; the
  country data on the data tabs. The formula of every row is listed in `excel_ai/mitigation/docs/Formulas.md`.
- **CPAT Python:** package `coded/cpat_model/`. The run is `cpat_model.run()` (`core/loop.py`); the order of the
  blocks is written once, in `mitigation/chain.py`; the blocks are in `mitigation/` and `distribution/`.
:::

## How a run is organised {#sec-ov-run}

A run takes one **scenario set** and a choice of countries, and returns every result by output code, country,
scenario and year.

### Countries, scenarios and scenario sets {#sec-ov-scenarios}

A **scenario** is one full column of inputs: one value for each policy input (the rows of legacy MTInputs and
Excel-AI's additions). A **scenario set** is a table of such columns, numbered from 1.

- **Scenario 1 is the baseline** ($o = B$): no new policy, only what the price data already contain (existing
  taxes, subsidies and carbon pricing).
- **Scenarios 2 to $n$ are policy scenarios** ($o = P$). Each runs with the same equations and its own inputs.

In Excel-AI each scenario is a **group of year columns** on the Mitigation sheet: group 1 is the baseline and
group 2 the live policy scenario. In CPAT Python a scenario set is a CSV file (`data/inputs/scenarios_<name>.csv`,
one column per scenario), and any number of scenarios run one after another.

A few inputs are read from the **baseline column for every scenario**: they are run settings, not policies. They
include the results year, the last historical price year, the social cost of carbon settings, the effectiveness of
output-based allocation, the price-control (pass-through) choice and the price floor.

### Baseline and comparisons {#sec-ov-baseline}

Most results are reported against the baseline. Write $X^{B}$ for the value of $X$ in the baseline (scenario 1)
in the same year and country. The **change against the baseline** is

$$
\Delta X_t = X_t - X^{B}_t
$$ {#eq-ov-delta}

where $X$ is any result (fuel use, CO2, revenue, GDP) and $t$ the year. Percent changes are
$\Delta X_t / X^{B}_t$.

Policy scenarios also *read* some baseline values as inputs: the baseline CO2 by ETS sector (for the ETS cap), the
calibration values of the GHG inventory year, and the same-year baseline revenue (for the fiscal space and so for
GDP in the next year). This is why the baseline always runs first.

### Years {#sec-ov-years}

The model runs **year by year from the base year $t_0$ to 2041**.

| Symbol | Year | Default | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| $t_0$ | Base year | 2022 | First year of the model. Fuel use is data in $t_0$ and modelled from $t_0 + 1$ |
| $L$ | Last historical price year | 2024 | Prices up to $L$ come from the price data; later years are projected (@sec-prices) |
| $Y$ | Last GHG inventory year of the country | data | Calibration of emissions (@sec-emissions) |
| $R$ | Results year | 2026 | The year of the real US dollars of every money value |
| $T_x$ | Last data year of existing carbon pricing | 2025 | Existing carbon taxes and ETS: data 2021-2025, then grown |
| — | Last year | 2041 | End of the projection (the legacy horizon of the power block) |
| — | Distribution analysis year | input `YearDistn` | The one year in which household effects are computed |

The macro series of the header (block M0) run over a longer range, the **macro years 2018 to 2045**, so that
growth rates and averages of earlier years exist.

### Money: the results year and real USD {#sec-ov-money}

**Every money value is in real US dollars of the results year $R$** (input `ResultsYear`, read from the baseline
column; 2026 by default), per unit of the quantity (USD/GJ, USD/tCO2, USD million). A constant real price is a
constant number: there is no inflation in the projection, and fuel use responds only to real price changes.

Two indices, both equal to 1 in $R$, convert nominal values to real ones (block M0, @eq-ov-indices):

- the **CPI index** $\nu_t$ (US consumer prices) converts nominal *domestic* values: the price data, existing
  taxes, the nominal option of the carbon price, producer subsidies;
- the **deflator index** $\delta_t$ (US GDP deflator) converts nominal *international* prices and GDP.

Policy inputs are real (results-year USD) unless an input says otherwise: only the carbon price has a nominal option.
The methodology describes the currency rules in its user guide
([methodology, section 1.2.11](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/01_User_Guide.html#currency-used-in-cpat)).

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Differences from legacy CPAT"}
- **Two indices, as legacy.** Legacy uses the CPI for domestic values and the deflator for international prices;
  the model keeps that split. Up to 2030 the two differ by up to 1.2% (2022: 1.137 against 1.124; 2030: 0.918
  against 0.929), so a single index would not reproduce legacy.
- **Horizon.** Legacy holds the US CPI flat after the WEO horizon (2031) but not the deflator; so does the model.
  The model computes to 2041, the horizon of the legacy power block; values after 2030 were not a target of the
  comparisons with legacy.
:::

## The calculation chain {#sec-ov-chain}

The model never solves a system of equations. Each year reads only that year and earlier years, so the whole run
is one pass in a fixed order. This section gives that order; each later chapter explains one link of it.

### Three stages, baseline first {#sec-ov-stages}

Each scenario runs in three stages.

1. **Prepare (all years at once).** Everything that depends on no model quantity: the macro header, the policy
   paths, the international and retail prices before and after policies, the power cost paths (including the
   forward-looking levelised costs). Because prices and policies are known for all years before any quantity is
   computed, a later year's price can be used in an earlier year's decision without a circular reference.
2. **Year loop ($t = t_0, \dots, 2041$).** Every block of the year, in a fixed order. The base year sets the
   starting values.
3. **Finish (all years).** Rows that need the whole path: the NDC targets and the gap.

The baseline runs first, then each policy scenario in turn, because policy scenarios read baseline values. After
all scenarios, the **distribution** module computes household effects in its analysis year, every scenario against
the baseline.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  P["Prepare, all years<br/>macro header, policies, prices, power cost paths"]
  subgraph YL["Year loop, t = t0 ... 2041"]
    direction LR
    G["GDP level<br/>of t"] --> PW["Power"] --> FU["Fuel use"] --> EM["Emissions"] --> RV["Revenues"] --> GE["GDP effect<br/>of t"]
  end
  F["Finish, all years: NDC gap"]
  D["Distribution: analysis year, deciles"]
  P --> YL
  GE -. "GDP of t+1" .-> G
  YL --> F --> D
  style YL fill:#f3f6fa,stroke:#8a9bb0,color:#1a1a1a
  classDef blk fill:#ffffff,stroke:#4a6a8a,color:#1a1a1a
  class P,G,PW,FU,EM,RV,GE,F,D blk
```

### One year of the loop {#sec-ov-year}

Within a year the blocks run in this order (CPAT Python `mitigation/chain.py`; Excel-AI computes the same rows, each
year reading only that year and earlier years).

| Step | Block | What it computes | Chapter |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | GDP level | Real GDP of year $t$, from the GDP effect of $t-1$ | @sec-fiscal |
| 2 | Power | Electricity demand (at last year's price), dispatch, retirement, investment, electricity prices, power revenues | @sec-power |
| 3 | Fuel use | Fuel use by subsector and fuel, biofuels, leakage to biomass, and their emissions and revenues | @sec-demand |
| 4 | Totals | Energy totals by sector group and fuel; prices averaged over fuel use | @sec-demand, @sec-prices |
| 5 | Emissions | CO2 and the ETS cap check; other greenhouse gases and methane; local air pollutants | @sec-emissions |
| 6 | Revenues | Revenue totals and revenue in percent of GDP | @sec-fiscal |
| 7 | Indicators | Kaya indices, carbon-pricing indicators, air-pollution costs | @sec-emissions, @sec-fiscal |
| 8 | GDP effect | Fiscal impulse, multipliers, GDP effect of year $t$; external balance | @sec-fiscal |
| 9 | Road | Road engineer model (when chosen), transport externalities | @sec-transport |
| 10 | Welfare, modules | Welfare gains, subsidies, efficient prices; the year step of the air-pollution and transport co-benefit modules | @sec-fiscal |

Two links run across years. The **GDP effect** of year $t$ moves the GDP level of year $t+1$ (the only feedback from
policy to activity). **Power** reads last year's electricity price for demand, and its capacities and vintages are
recursions on $t-1$. The only look-aheads read exogenous paths built in the prepare stage, such as the levelised
variable cost of power over $[t, 2041]$.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: a run"}
```
settings = run_settings(scenario_set.column(1))       # results year, last price year, ... from the baseline
for o in [1, 2, ..., n]:                              # baseline first
    state = {}
    for block in PREPARE:                             # header, policies, prices, power costs, fuel prices, ...
        block(state, inputs[o], baseline)             # all years at once
    for t in range(base_year, 2041 + 1):
        for block in YEAR:                            # gdp.start, power.step, fuel_use.step, totals, emissions,
            block(state, inputs[o], baseline, t)      # revenues, indicators, gdp.effects, road, welfare, ...
    for block in FINISH:                              # NDC gap
        block(state, inputs[o], baseline)
    if o == 1:
        baseline = state                              # read by every policy scenario
    results[o] = state
if 'YearDistn' in inputs[1]:
    results.distribution = distribution(results, year=YearDistn)   # every scenario against the baseline
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** sheet Mitigation computes every row for every year in its scenario groups: group 1 is the baseline,
  group 2 the live scenario (each group is 22 columns wide: the code column, the years 2022-2041 and a spacer;
  constant `MitGW`). Each year reads only that year and earlier years. Baseline values that policy scenarios read are
  stored on sheet BaselineCO2 (CO2 by ETS sector, methane activity). Sheet Distribution reads both groups.
- **CPAT Python:** `core/loop.py` (`run_scenarios`, `run_one`); the stages are the lists `PREPARE`, `YEAR` and
  `FINISH` of `mitigation/chain.py`. Every function works on all countries at once (an array dimension). Each block
  and its tests are listed in [the blocks](../CPAT_coded_documentation_html/02_How_it_works.html#sec-blocks).
- **Outside the passes**, in both: the ETS goal seek, which repeats whole runs until emissions meet the cap (only on
  request; @sec-emissions).
:::

## Index sets {#sec-ov-indices}

Every variable of the model is indexed by some of a few dimensions. The notation follows the methodology
([methodology, section 3.1.9.1](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#sec-ExecSummDimensions)); where
it has no symbol, the symbol of the Excel-AI equation note is used.

| Index | Dimension | Elements |
|---|---|---|
| $o$ | Scenario | $B$ baseline (scenario 1), $P$ a policy scenario (2 to $n$) |
| $c$ | Country | ISO3 code (`EGY`, ...) |
| $u$ | UNFCCC emissions sector | Energy, industrial processes, agriculture, land use, waste, other |
| $g$ | Sector group | Mitigation: power, transport, buildings, industry, other energy use. Prices: power, residential, industry |
| $s$ | Sector | The 16 subsectors; power where a policy covers it (17 coverage sectors) |
| $f$ | Fuel, or generation type in power | 9 fuels; 9 generation types |
| $p$ | Pollutant | CO2, CH4, N2O, F-gases; local pollutants |
| $t$ | Year | $t_0$ to 2041 |

**Indices are omitted where they add nothing.** Every equation holds for each scenario $o$ and country $c$, and for
each year $t$ unless $t$ is shown; they are left out unless needed. A previous-year value carries $t-1$; a baseline
value of the same year carries the superscript $B$.

### Sectors {#sec-ov-sectors}

The 16 subsectors $s$ and the groupings each block uses. The **sector group** aggregates energy and emissions. The
**price sector** says which coal and gas price a subsector pays. The **feebate group** and **ETS group** say which
feebate rate and ETS benchmark apply (power is a sector of its own for both). The **semi-elasticity group** picks the
ETS semi-elasticity.

| Code | Subsector | Sector group | Coal and gas price sector | Feebate and ETS group | ETS semi-elasticity group |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `rod` | Road | Transport | Residential | Transport | Transport |
| `ral` | Rail | Transport | Industry | Transport | Transport |
| `avi` | Domestic aviation | Transport | Industry | Transport | Transport |
| `nav` | Domestic navigation | Transport | Industry | Transport | Transport |
| `res` | Residential | Buildings | Residential | Residential | Residential |
| `foo` | Food and forestry | Buildings | Industry | Residential | Industry |
| `srv` | Services (public and private) | Buildings | Industry | Residential | Industry |
| `mch` | Mining and chemicals | Industry | Industry | Industry | Industry |
| `irn` | Iron and steel | Industry | Industry | Industry | Industry |
| `nfm` | Other metals | Industry | Industry | Industry | Industry |
| `mac` | Machinery | Industry | Industry | Industry | Industry |
| `cem` | Cement | Industry | Industry | Industry | Industry |
| `omn` | Other manufacturing | Industry | Industry | Industry | Industry |
| `cst` | Construction | Industry | Industry | Industry | Industry |
| `ftr` | Fuel transformation | Industry | Industry | Industry | Industry |
| `oen` | Other energy use | Other energy use | Industry | Industry | Industry |

Power (`pow`) is the 17th **coverage sector**: carbon tax, ETS and feebate coverage switches exist for power and
for each subsector.

### Fuels and price blocks {#sec-ov-fuels}

Fuel use is kept for 9 fuels $f$. Prices are kept by **price block**: a fuel in a price sector, as in the IMF price
dataset ([methodology, section 3.2.2](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#sec-PricesNotation)). Coal
and gas have one price for each of power, residential and industry; oil products and biomass one price for all
sectors. Electricity prices come from the power block, by user group.

| Code | Fuel | Price unit | GJ per price unit | Price blocks |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `coa` | Coal | USD/GJ | 1 | power, residential, industry |
| `nga` | Natural gas | USD/GJ | 1 | power, residential, industry |
| `gso` | Gasoline | USD/liter | 0.03497 | all sectors |
| `die` | Diesel | USD/liter | 0.03730 | all sectors |
| `lpg` | LPG | USD/liter | 0.02578 | all sectors |
| `ker` | Kerosene | USD/liter | 0.03775 | all sectors |
| `jfu` | Jet fuel | USD/liter | 0.03486 | takes the kerosene block |
| `oop` | Other oil products | USD/bbl | 6.12 | all sectors |
| `bio` | Biomass | USD/GJ | 1 | all sectors |

This gives **12 price blocks** $(g, f)$ for fuels; the fuel price reform adds two electricity blocks (residential,
industry), 14 in all. The equation list writes a price block with the single index $c$; this book writes $(g, f)$,
to keep $c$ for the country.

### Power, electricity users, distribution {#sec-ov-other-indices}

| Index | Set | Elements |
|---|---|---|
| $f$ in power | Generation types (9) | Coal, gas, oil, nuclear, wind, solar, hydro, other renewables, biomass |
| User group | Electricity price groups (2) | Residential, industry |
| Demand group | Electricity demand groups (4) | Transport, residential, industry, services |
| ECP sector $j$ | Existing carbon pricing sectors (4) | Power, transport, residential, industry |
| $k$ | Phase-outs (3) | Producer subsidies, consumer subsidies, price controls |
| Distribution | (chapter @sec-distribution) | Household $j$, decile $d$, consumption category $g$, fuel $f \in g$, analysis year $y$ |

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Notation clashes to keep in mind"}
The methodology reuses some letters, and so does this book where it follows the methodology:

- $g$ is the sector group in mitigation, generation in the methodology's power chapter, and the consumption
  category in distribution. This book uses $g$ for sector groups, and for categories only in distribution.
- $E$ is both electricity and the energy UNFCCC sector in the methodology.
- $\gamma$ is a generation share in the methodology's power chapter and the pass-through in distribution.
- $u$ is the UNFCCC sector in the methodology; the equation list also uses it for the electricity user groups.
- $d$ is the electricity demand group in the Excel-AI equation note and the decile in distribution.
- $j$ is the ECP sector here and the household in distribution.
- The Excel-AI equation note writes $c$ for a price fuel, $k$ for a generation type and $e$ for a coverage sector;
  this book writes $(g,f)$, $f$ and $s$.
:::

## Units and unit constants {#sec-ov-units}

The model uses the units of legacy CPAT, not a fully consistent SI system
([methodology, section 3.1.9.5](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#sec-ExecSummUnits);
[user guide, section 1.2.12](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/01_User_Guide.html#energy-units-in-cpat)).

| Quantity | Unit |
|---|---|
| Fuel use (final and primary energy) | ktoe per year |
| Electricity demand and generation | GWh per year; MWy (megawatt-years) inside the power dispatch |
| Capacity | MW |
| Fuel prices, taxes, subsidies, carbon prices per unit of energy | real USD/GJ (inputs in price units: USD/liter, USD/bbl, USD/GJ) |
| Electricity prices and costs | real USD/kWh |
| Carbon prices, feebates, methane fee | real USD/tCO2, USD/tCO2e |
| Revenues | real USD million |
| GDP | real USD billion |
| CO2 and other greenhouse gases | MtCO2, MtCO2e |
| Methane | kt CH4 |
| Local air pollutants | kt |

**Unit constants.** The model converts between these units with the constants of sheet Constants (Excel-AI) and
`core/excel_ai/constants.csv` (CPAT Python). The ones used throughout are:

| Symbol | Constant | Value |
|---|---|---|
| $\theta$ | PJ per ktoe | 0.041868 |
| $H$ | Hours per year (`HoursYr`) | 8760 |
| $\theta_e$ | GJ per kWh (`GJperkWh`) | 0.0036 |
| $M$ | Million kWh per MW-year (`MWyMkWh`) | 8.76 |
| $\theta_g$ | GWh per ktoe (`KtoeGWh`) | 11.63 |
| — | t per kt, kt per Mt (`tPerKt`, `ktPerMt`) | 1000 |
| — | USD million per USD billion (`MperBn`) | 1000 |
| — | Liters per barrel (`LitersPerBbl`) | 158.987 |
| — | Liters of crude oil per ktoe (`LitersPerKtoeOil`) | 1,108,792 |
| — | Global warming potential of methane, fossil and non-fossil (`GWPCH4F`, `GWPCH4NF`) | 29.8, 27.2 tCO2e per t CH4 |
| — | Floor of the after-tax fuel price (`PriceFloor`) | 0.01 USD/GJ |

Since fuel use is in ktoe and prices are in USD/GJ, a fuel use times a price per GJ times $\theta$ is in USD million:

$$
\text{revenue (USD million)} = F\,[\text{ktoe}] \times \theta\,[\text{PJ/ktoe}] \times \tau\,[\text{USD/GJ}]
$$ {#eq-ov-revenue-units}

because one PJ is a million GJ. Similarly, a cost in USD/kWh times a generation in MWy times $M$ is in USD million.

## Conventions {#sec-ov-conventions}

A few conventions hold in every chapter.

- **Indicator.** $\mathbb{1}[\cdot]$ is 1 if the condition holds and 0 otherwise. For example
  $\mathbb{1}[o \ne B]$ is 1 in a policy scenario.
- **Switches.** Yes/No inputs are switches of the scenario. A text switch counts as Yes when it *starts* with
  "Yes" (so "Yes" and "Yes*" both count; the test is on the first three letters, ignoring case). A tick box is TRUE
  or FALSE; in arithmetic TRUE is 1 and FALSE or a blank cell is 0.
- **Defaults.** An asterisk marks the default option of a dropdown input ("Medium*", "Real*", "Linear*"). Numbers in
  parentheses in the parameter tables of this book are defaults of sheet Constants or Settings, not country data.
- **Blank inputs** read as 0, as an Excel lookup of an empty cell does.
- **Baseline and previous year.** $X^{B}_t$ is the baseline value in the same year; $X_{t-1}$ the value of the
  previous year in the same scenario.
- **Codes.** Every variable has a short code (`ener`, `atp`, `cptraj`, ...), the same in Excel-AI (row codes) and
  CPAT Python (variable names). A full output code adds the country, module, sector, fuel and scenario, for example
  `egy.mit.co2.tot.tot.2`.
- **Equation ids.** Each equation of the model has an id (M1.2, A2.5, ...) in the equation lists of the appendices;
  CPAT Python cites it in the code (`EQ-M1.2`). This book links them, for example
  ([M1.1](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M1-1)).

## Header: the macro series (M0) {#sec-ov-header}

The header turns the IMF World Economic Outlook (WEO) data of the country into the series every later block reads:
the price indices that make money values real, real GDP in US dollars and local currency, the exchange rate and the
baseline growth of GDP. It depends on no model quantity, so it is computed for all years in the prepare stage.
The methodology lists the macro data and their sources in
[methodology, section 3.9.1](../CPAT_full_documentation_html/03_Mitigation.html#appendix-a---macro-data-of-cpat-sources-and-codes).

### Macro series past the last data year {#sec-ov-macro-extension}

Each WEO series is data up to its own last data year $T^{WEO}_x$ and is then extended by a rule of its own
([M0.1](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M0-1)):

$$
x_t = \begin{cases} x^{WEO}_t & t \le T^{WEO}_x \\ \text{extension rule of } x & t > T^{WEO}_x \end{cases}
$$ {#eq-ov-macro}

over the macro years 2018 to 2045. The rules are:

| Series | WEO code | Extension past the last data year |
|---|---|---|
| US GDP deflator | `USA.NGDP_D` | Linear trend: $x_t = 2x_{t-1} - x_{t-2}$ |
| US CPI | `USA.PCPI` | Held flat: $x_t = x_{t-1}$ |
| Real GDP growth | `NGDP_RPCH` | Held, or eased off when falling (@eq-ov-growth) |
| Real GDP, local currency | `NGDP_R` | Grown with real growth: $x_t = x_{t-1}(1 + g_t)$ |
| Nominal GDP, local currency | `NGDP` | Grown with its last growth rate, held from the last data year |
| Nominal GDP, USD | `NGDPD` | Grown with the nominal growth rate of local-currency GDP |
| Exchange rate | `XDC_USD.PA_RT` | Held flat; a euro country takes the euro area's rate (WEO `G163`) |
| Population | `LP` | Grown with its last growth factor: $x_t = x_{t-1}\,x_{t-1}/x_{t-2}$ |

Real GDP growth is held at its last value, unless it was falling. Then it eases off: it keeps at least half of the
average of the last three years, and otherwise follows the linear trend of the last two:

$$
g_t = \begin{cases} g_{t-1} & g_{t-1} \ge g_{t-2} \\[4pt] \max\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\,\bar{g}_{t-3..t-1},\; 2g_{t-1} - g_{t-2}\right) & g_{t-1} < g_{t-2} \end{cases}
$$ {#eq-ov-growth}

where

- $g_t$ is real GDP growth in year $t$ (share per year);
- $\bar{g}_{t-3..t-1}$ is the average of the growth rates of the three previous years;
- $\tfrac{1}{2}$ is the constant `GdpExtHalf` (0.5).

Nominal GDP in local currency grows with the growth rate of its last data year; in Excel-AI that rate is the one
of the year before the last data year, and CPAT Python does the same.

### Price indices, real GDP and the exchange rate {#sec-ov-indices-macro}

The header rows of the model read these series ([M0.2](A_Equations.qmd#eqlist-M0-2)):

$$
\nu_t = \frac{CPI^{US}_{R}}{CPI^{US}_t}, \qquad \delta_t = \frac{D^{US}_{R}}{D^{US}_t}
$$ {#eq-ov-indices}

where

- $\nu_t$ (`infl`) is the CPI index: it converts nominal domestic prices and nominal policy inputs of year $t$ to
  real USD of $R$;
- $\delta_t$ (`defl`) is the deflator index: it converts nominal international prices;
- $CPI^{US}_t$, $D^{US}_t$ are the US CPI and GDP deflator (WEO, extended as above);
- $R$ is the results year.

Both indices equal 1 in $R$, are above 1 before it and below 1 after it.

Real GDP in US dollars (`gdp.usd`, USD billion of $R$) is converted from nominal GDP in the historical years and grown
with real growth from the base year on:

$$
Y^{USD}_t = \begin{cases} \dfrac{Y^{n}_t}{e^{n}_t}\,\delta_t & t < t_0 \\[8pt] Y^{USD}_{t-1}\,(1 + g_t) & t \ge t_0 \end{cases}
$$ {#eq-ov-gdp-usd}

where $Y^{n}_t$ is nominal GDP in local currency, $e^{n}_t$ the market exchange rate (local currency per USD) and
$g_t$ real GDP growth (`gdp.base`, the baseline growth that the GDP block starts from; @sec-fiscal).

Real GDP in local currency (`gdp.lcu`) is the WEO real GDP series, $Y^{LCU}_t = Y^{R}_t$. The **exchange rate the
model uses** is the ratio of the two real GDP series:

$$
e_t = \frac{Y^{LCU}_t}{Y^{USD}_t}
$$ {#eq-ov-xr}

in local currency per real US dollar (`xr`). From the base year on both series grow at the same rate, so $e_t$ is
constant in real terms. GDP per capita is $Y^{USD}_t$ divided by population (times 1000, population being in
thousands).

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="Pseudocode: the macro header"}
```
for c in countries:
    for x in [ngdp_d(USA), pcpi(USA), gdp_growth, ngdp_r, ngdp, ngdpd, xr, lp]:
        for y in range(2018, 2045 + 1):
            if y <= last_data_year[x]:
                x[y] = weo[x][y]                         # euro countries: xr from the euro area (G163)
            else:
                x[y] = extension_rule[x](x[y-1], x[y-2], ...)
    for y in macro_years:                                # gdp_growth when falling:
        ...                                              #   max(0.5 * mean(g[y-3..y-1]), 2*g[y-1] - g[y-2])
    for t in years:
        infl[t] = pcpi[R] / pcpi[t]                      # CPI index, 1 in the results year
        defl[t] = ngdp_d[R] / ngdp_d[t]                  # deflator index
        if t < base_year:
            gdp_usd[t] = ngdp[t] / xr_market[t] * defl[t]
        else:
            gdp_usd[t] = gdp_usd[t-1] * (1 + gdp_growth[t])
        gdp_lcu[t] = ngdp_r[t]
        xr[t] = gdp_lcu[t] / gdp_usd[t]                  # real LCU per real USD
        gdp_base[t] = gdp_growth[t]
```
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="In Excel-AI and CPAT Python"}
- **Excel-AI:** the macro series are built on sheet Inputs_macro (the data step of legacy Mitigation rows 417-467);
  the header rows `infl`, `defl`, `gdp.usd`, `gdp.lcu`, `xr` and the GDP growth rows are Mitigation section 0
  (rows 8-13; formulas E1-E6 of `Formulas.md`). The results year is ScenarioDefinition `ResultsYear` of scenario 1.
- **CPAT Python:** `cpat_model/mitigation/header.py`, `prepare()` (`macro_series()` for the extensions,
  `_header()` for the rows); equations M0.1, M0.2. The series are stored as `macro.<series>`; the result is cached
  and shared by the runs of one baseline.
:::

The header block matches Excel-AI's stored values for Egypt in every scenario and year (CPAT Python test block
"3.1 header"; no known differences). Values of the shipped scenario set (results year 2026):

| Year | 2022 | 2025 | 2026 | 2027 | 2030 | 2035 | 2041 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CPI index $\nu_t$ | 1.1368 | 1.0323 | 1.0000 | 0.9790 | 0.9175 | 0.8979 | 0.8979 |
| Deflator index $\delta_t$ | 1.1242 | 1.0286 | 1.0000 | 0.9785 | 0.9288 | 0.8519 | 0.7749 |
| Real GDP (USD bn of 2026) | 547.0 | 606.7 | 632.4 | 662.9 | 771.8 | 970.3 | 1255.6 |
| Baseline real GDP growth | 6.65% | 4.39% | 4.24% | 4.83% | 4.84% | 4.58% | 4.26% |

The CPI index is flat from 2031 (the US CPI is held flat after the WEO horizon); the deflator is not. The exchange
rate is 14.34 Egyptian pounds per real US dollar in every year.
